title: Nothing great without enthusiasm
hookLine: nothing great was ever achieved without enthusiasm (Circles)

cards: Emerson has spent all of Circles saying that nothing stays settled. Every idea gets outgrown. Every wall turns out to have a door in it.

A reader can come out of it a little dizzy, wondering what's left to stand on. Then, near the close, he sets down one sentence like a flag in the ground: "Nothing great was ever achieved without enthusiasm." Not talent.
Not a plan. Not the right people. Enthusiasm.
It can sound like a pep rally, or a job listing for an enthusiastic self-starter. Emerson means something larger and stranger.

teach.b: First, where the line sits. Just before it, Emerson names what he thinks people want almost more than anything: to forget ourselves, to be surprised out of our good manners, to do something without knowing how or why.
In his words, "to draw a new circle." Enthusiasm is the force that carries a person past the edge of the old circle. Second, it's a kind of letting go.

teach.h: THE WAY OF LIFE IS ABANDONMENT.
teach.b: Right after the line, he says the way of life goes by abandonment: not careful steps, but being taken over by something. A musician who stops counting and starts playing.

A child so deep in a sandcastle that dinner gets called three times. Third, it isn't noise. A gardener on her knees at dawn, wholly inside the work, may have more of it than someone shouting at a game.
It's whether the self-watching part of you has gone quiet because the thing in front of you is bigger. Fourth, the ordinary day.
A lot of a day gets done at half power, one eye on the clock, one eye on how we look.
Emerson's claim is that nothing great comes out of that state. Small things can be done the other way too: a meal, a letter, a walk, a conversation, given the whole of you for a few minutes.

how: Readers of Emerson often quote this line from Circles alongside the passage just before it, about the wish to forget ourselves and draw a new circle, as a call to throw oneself fully into work and life.

games.q: what does “nothing great without enthusiasm” mean?
o: careful planning that keeps every step under control
the absorbed force that carries you past your old limits
a cheerful, upbeat mood you put on for other people

s: Emerson's enthusiasm means being loud and upbeat
it can be very quiet. the test is absorption, not volume.
just before the line, Emerson speaks of wanting to forget ourselves
he describes the wish to be surprised out of ourselves and "to draw a new circle."
the line comes from Emerson's essay on self-reliance
it comes near the end of Circles.

games.q: you've written a whole essay saying every idea gets outgrown and nothing stays settled. how do you end it?
o: with a warning to play it safe.
with a plea to keep the old circle.
games.why: Emerson ends near this line: "nothing great was ever achieved without enthusiasm." the unsettling essay closes by pointing at what carries us forward.

practice: Bring to mind one ordinary task ahead of you: washing a pan, answering a message, walking to the car.

Picture doing it with your whole attention, the way the child is inside the sandcastle, noticing how your hands move and what you hear. No forced cheer, just all of you, for the length of one small task.

wordCard.voice: Nothing great without enthusiasm. The line near the end of Emerson's Circles: the force that carries us past the old circle, by letting go rather than holding back. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: with enthusiasm. Quiet absorption counts as much as loud cheer. See you tomorrow.
